ui._doc_screensaver: The Screensaver (ScreensaverService) — a full-screen OPAQUE BLACK overlay (SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW), NOT an Activity and NOT a lock: the app underneath stays resumed, so a playing video/audio keeps going, just hidden. Shows the time + date at the top and an Unlock button at the bottom (the only actionable). Triggered by the floating-nav `screensaver` action. `time_format`/`date_format` are java.text.SimpleDateFormat patterns; `unlock_label` is the dismiss button text.
ui._doc_screensavers: Configs → Launcher → Screensaver picker. LauncherSettingsPrefs persists the choice; ScreensaverService renders the chosen mode (clock formats from ui.screensaver). 'black_clock' = the classic OPAQUE BLACK clock+date+unlock. 'neon_lights' = animated neon scene behind the same clock. default:true = first-run choice.

screensavers.label: Black Clock
screensavers.subtitle: All-black: time + date + unlock. The classic.

screensavers.label: Neon Lights
screensavers.subtitle: Animated neon grid glowing behind the clock.

ui._doc_launcher_settings: Configs → Launcher → Others. Data-driven toggles + sliders persisted via LauncherSettingsPrefs, read by each subsystem at runtime. toggles[].id maps to a pref key; default = first-run value. Sliders carry min/max and either a `default` or, where the row offers one-tap sizes, a `presets` list whose `shipped` entry IS the default (scale, #408 — never both, or the two copies drift). brightness.default -1 = leave system brightness untouched. Adding a toggle = one entry here + one subsystem read.

toggles.label: All animations
toggles.subtitle: Master switch - off stops every animation.

toggles.label: Animal animations
toggles.subtitle: Animate the status-bar pets.

toggles.label: Cube animation
toggles.subtitle: 3D home cube motion.

toggles.label: Cube drag-to-spin
toggles.subtitle: Touch and drag the home cube to spin it across its 3D faces.

toggles.label: Island animation
toggles.subtitle: Home-screen island wave motion.

toggles.label: Stars animation
toggles.subtitle: Galaxy backdrop stars + comets.

toggles.label: Live system stats
toggles.subtitle: Refresh RAM/CPU/storage every 10s (off = frozen numbers, leaner).

toggles.label: Star twinkle
toggles.subtitle: Pulse the home Sirius star (off = static).

toggles.label: Store update check
toggles.subtitle: Periodic GHCR check for sibling-app updates (off = manual only, saves network).
toggles._doc: WorkManager tag superapp-updater-check. This toggle already existed and already LIED: background_pause cancelled the job while the switch still read ON. Moving it into Connectivity and mapping it from the theme is what makes the switch agree with the device.

toggles.label: Vibration on tap
toggles.subtitle: Haptic feedback on every tap.

toggles.label: Eye protection
toggles.subtitle: Warm amber overlay to cut blue light.

toggles._doc: features.home_3d. The theme has always flipped this and there was no switch for it, so a user in Power Saving could not get the cube back without abandoning the whole theme.
toggles.label: 3D home pane
toggles.subtitle: The rotating cube home screen (off = the flat app grid).

toggles._doc: features.dynamic_island. Same defect as home_3d: theme-flipped, never exposed.
toggles.label: Dynamic island
toggles.subtitle: The floating pill above the toolbar.

toggles._doc: features.oled_black. ShellActivity paints the decor view black for this; the user had no way to keep the black background while leaving the theme.
toggles.label: OLED black background
toggles.subtitle: Pure black window background — an OLED panel spends no power on black pixels.

toggles._doc: features.background_pause — the single most invisible thing a theme did. BackgroundOrchestrator.applyForTheme cancels the WorkManager tags and stops the Maps tracker, and NOTHING on screen said so. The three jobs it cancels each have their own switch below, so this is the master and they are the detail.
toggles.label: Pause background work
toggles.subtitle: Tear down the location tracker, the update poll and the message poll.

toggles._doc: PhoneAppsFragment.warmUp is skipped under background_pause. The cost of it being off is a slow Phone tab, which reads as a bug rather than a setting.
toggles.label: Warm up the app list
toggles.subtitle: Pre-index installed apps at launch so the Phone tab opens instantly.

toggles._doc: BackgroundOrchestrator.stopMapsTracker. A location service the user cannot see stopping is the one they most need told about.
toggles.label: Location tracking
toggles.subtitle: Keep the Maps location service running in the background.

toggles._doc: features.wireguard_required. This is the one thing Power Saving turns ON rather than off, and it deserves a switch precisely because it is surprising: a power-saving mode that keeps a VPN up is a deliberate choice, not a leak.
toggles.label: Keep WireGuard up
toggles.subtitle: Pin the tunnel ON — connectivity survives power saving.

toggles._doc: WorkManager tag superapp-ntfy-poll. Cancelled by background_pause, which means Power Saving silently stopped delivering notifications. This is the toggle the Notifications group exists for.
toggles.label: Message polling
toggles.subtitle: Poll the ntfy server for new messages and notifications.

toggles._doc: WorkManager tag superapp-analytics-batch, the third job background_pause cancels.
toggles.label: Usage batch upload
toggles.subtitle: Send batched usage events when the network is idle.

toggles._doc: features.bottom_nav. Chrome rather than battery, but still theme-flipped with no switch.
toggles.label: Bottom navigation bar
toggles.subtitle: The section bar along the bottom of the screen.

toggles.label: Side drawer
toggles.subtitle: The slide-in section drawer.

toggles._doc: PART FOUR, and the one toggle a THEME MAY NOT TOUCH. `user_owned: true` is not documentation — LauncherThemes.parseToggles DROPS this id out of every theme's mapping at parse time, so a theme cannot force edge menus off even if someone adds `"edge_menus": false` to its record by mistake. The owner asked to keep edge menus while in power saving; a theme that could stomp it would take the feature away exactly when one-handed use matters most. Backed by OneHandPrefs (store `onehand_prefs`), NOT by launcher_settings — the One-Hand tab writes the same key, so the two surfaces agree.
toggles.label: Edge menus
toggles.subtitle: One-Hand edge gesture pads on the screen borders.

toggles._doc: Samsung exposes light/dark as a system-wide setting, not an app one, so this is NOT AppCompatDelegate.setDefaultNightMode — that would repaint this app alone and leave the phone half light. Backed by store `nightmode`, which runs `cmd uimode night yes|no` over the shell channel, i.e. it needs the same SHELL authority the Battery Hunger levers need. Dark is the default: every mode this launcher ships is a dark design.
toggles.label: Dark mode
toggles.subtitle: System-wide light/dark — needs the shell channel.

launcher_settings._doc_scale: One knob for the two levers Samsung splits in two: Screen zoom (`wm density`) and Font size (`settings put system font_scale`). Both take the SAME factor, 0.70 + 0.05 x scale, so 6 is exactly 1.00 and changes nothing — which is why 6 is the step the owner named 'Normal'. It is no longer the SHIPPED step: #408 moved that to 3 (factor 0.85), declared as the `shipped` preset below. Scale 1 is the minimum on both. Density multiplies the panel's physical number; font_scale is absolute. Anything that writes these must remember the override it clobbers.

scale._doc: #384: the owner asked for 0-10, not #337's 1-10, and for a slider that can only sit ON a step. `ticks` draws one mark per step under the line (SeekBar.setTickMark, API 24+) and makes the current level readable; the buttons on this row read `presets` from HERE, so the shipped size is declared once. RANGE CONSEQUENCE, stated rather than clamped away: SystemDisplay.factor is 0.70 + 0.05 * scale, so step 0 is factor 0.70 — a real, distinct, smallest step (30% smaller than the panel's own size), NOT a no-op and NOT an invisible UI. It is smaller than Android's own Screen-zoom floor, so it will look extreme; 6 is still exactly 1.00, the phone's own size, and Restore returns there in one tap. Before #384 step 0 would have been silently coerced to 1 and been pixel-identical to it, which is the one outcome a tick bar must never have.
scale.label: Scale
scale.subtitle: Whole UI, icons and text together. Default 3 = 0.85, Normal 6 = the phone's own size.
scale._doc_presets: #408. THE SHIPPED SIZE AND THE BUTTONS ARE ONE DECLARATION, and this key is why there is no `default` beside it any more. The owner asked for two one-tap sizes — 'Default' = 3 and 'Normal' = 6 — AND for a fresh install to land on 3. Written as a `default: 3` here plus a `3` in a button list, that is the same number in two places: widen or retune one and the install default and the button it is named after silently disagree, which is #384's defect exactly (its range was declared twice and folding one copy ate a whole step). So the preset flagged `shipped: true` IS the first-run value — LauncherSettingsPrefs.Config.slider() derives Slider.default from it, sp.getInt("scale", ...) falls back to it, and the button labels and their numbers are read off the same records. Moving the shipped size is editing one `shipped` flag. THE FACTORS, stated because the owner is choosing by eye and SystemDisplay.factor is 0.70 + 0.05 x scale: step 3 is 0.85 (15% smaller than the panel's own size) and step 6 is 1.00 (the phone's own size, where applyScale RESETS both levers instead of pinning them). Both are real, distinct, reachable steps of the declared 0..10 ladder. NOTE ON THE LABELS: 'Default' is the owner's word for 3 and 'Normal' is his word for 6, quoted verbatim from the ticket; they are not derived from which one is shipped, and renaming them is a data edit here.

screensaver_timeout.label: Screensaver timer
screensaver_timeout.subtitle: Auto-start the screensaver after N seconds idle (0 = never).

launcher_settings._doc_toggle_groups: The four boxes Configs > Launcher > Theme draws its switches into, in this order. A toggle names its group by id; the fragment renders one box per entry here and drops an empty one. This REPLACED a hardcoded Kotlin split (`toggles.filter { it.battery }` vs `!it.battery`) that could only ever express two groups, so a third box was a code change. Adding a fifth box is now one entry here plus a `group` on the toggles that belong in it.

toggle_groups.label: Launcher Battery Hungers
toggle_groups.subtitle: Continuous motion, the 3D home pane, live stats and background work — the effects that actually drain the cell. Off = leaner.
toggle_groups.master_subtitle: One switch to flip every effect below on or off.

toggle_groups.label: Connectivity
toggle_groups.subtitle: What the launcher keeps talking to the network about. Power Saving cuts compute but PINS the tunnel up, mirroring Samsung / Apple / Pixel power-save.

toggle_groups.label: Notifications
toggle_groups.subtitle: Delivery of messages the launcher pushes at you. Pausing background work silently stops these, which is why the switch has to be visible.

toggle_groups.label: Others
toggle_groups.subtitle: Chrome, haptics, eye protection and the edge menus — preferences that cost no battery worth naming.

launcher_settings._doc_feature_exposure: THE ANTI-INVISIBILITY CONTRACT. Every key in a theme's `features` block is a device state the theme changes behind the user's back, so every key must be accounted for here: either it maps to the id of the toggle that exposes it, or it is listed in `feature_not_toggleable` with the reason it is not a switch. The tester walks ui.launcher_themes and fails on any feature key that appears in neither, which is what stops the next feature flag from shipping with no way for the user to see or undo it — the defect this whole change exists to fix.

feature_not_toggleable.grid: A LAYOUT choice, not a device state. It names the shape of the home pane ('default', 'monospace_list') and each launcher theme declares its own, not a switch the user flips. A boolean could not express it and a switch labelled 'grid' would explain nothing.

launcher_settings._doc_background_jobs: The background work `background_pause` tears down, and the toggle that shows each piece of it. BackgroundOrchestrator cancels these WorkManager tags and stops the Maps tracker; before this list existed the user got no signal that notifications had stopped arriving. Keep in sync with BackgroundOrchestrator.TAGGED_JOBS — the tester asserts every entry here names a toggle that exists.

ui._doc_ai_routing_peers: THE FLEET AS Configs ▸ AI ▸ Tokens Fleet LISTS IT — which apps take part in AI Routing and what part each one plays. Baked to BuildConfig.UI_AI_ROUTING_PEERS_B64 and read by AiFleetRoster; a Kotlin list here would be exactly the hardcoded roster FIRE RULE #6 forbids. Each entry is {package, label, role}. WHETHER an app is installed and answering is NOT declared here and never could be — that is asked of the device at render time, of the package manager and of the binder.
ui._doc_ai_routing_peers_roles: `serves` = this app HOLDS the provider key and the model registry and answers ITextTools; there is exactly one, and it is the only place a key exists on the phone. `routes` = this app calls that binder to get work done and holds its OWN model choice but NO key of its own — cloud-mail is the one app in this state today. `console` = this app holds neither key nor route and exists to show and edit the others, which is what cloud-superapp is here; it is listed rather than omitted because the owner asked for the fleet view to include this app, and 'this app holds no key' is the honest answer to that, not a reason to leave the row out.
ui._doc_ai_routing_peers_drift: This roster is DECLARED and can therefore go stale, which FleetPeers deliberately avoids by treating an installed provider as the membership marker. The same trick does not work here: every constellation app ships that provider, so it would answer 'who is in the fleet' and not 'who does AI Routing', and every non-AI app would appear in this list with nothing to show. Adding an app to AI Routing means adding it here — one entry, no Kotlin.

ai_routing_peers._doc: The one key-holder. libs:keyboard owns AiRouter, the keyboard_ai registry and the PREF_AI_TOKEN_PREFIX slot, and serves TextToolsService under the signature-level CONSTELLATION_DATA permission. Every model, price and key Tokens Fleet shows is read from THIS app over that binder.
ai_routing_peers.label: cloud-keyboard

ai_routing_peers._doc: Routes through the keyboard and holds its own copy of the Enhance/Resume settings and its own model choice (build.json::mail_ai, MailTextToolsPrefs) — but NO key: it calls enhanceWith/summariseWith and the keyboard spends the credential. Its row says so rather than showing an empty key field that would read as a key it had lost.
ai_routing_peers.label: cloud-mail

ai_routing_peers._doc: Cloud Writer — the application the owner asked for, and the only peer with a MODEL PER TOOL: Text Enhance, Grammar Check and Summary each resolve their own, which is what "here we will define the AI model to do Summary, Grammar Only, Text Enhance" asked for. It routes exactly as Cloud Mail does — its own registry (ac_cloud-writer/build.json::writer_ai), its own composed prompts, its own provider, and NO key: it calls enhanceWith/summariseWith and the serving app spends the credential.
ai_routing_peers._doc_not_serves_yet: cloud-writer is FIRST in TextTools.SERVICE_PACKAGES, so it becomes the server the day its manifest publishes the ITextTools action — not the day this row is edited. This row reads `routes` because that APK does not publish it, for a reason no manifest can fix: the owner's provider key lives in cloud-keyboard's SharedPreferences under cloud-keyboard's uid and no install moves it, so a serving cloud-writer would take Enhance, Summary, Translate and Grammar from every consumer on its first bind and answer 'No API key' to all four. When it does serve, this row becomes `serves` and Cloud Keyboard's drops to `routes` IN THE SAME COMMIT — AiFleetRoster documents that exactly one app serves, and two `serves` rows with one real server makes this console report a peer that cannot answer.
ai_routing_peers.label: cloud-writer

ai_routing_peers._doc: This app. It holds no provider key and no route of its own — it links libs:text-tools only to ASK the keyboard about its routing state. Listed because the owner asked for the fleet view to include this app; 'holds no key, routes nothing, this is the console' is the true answer for it.
ai_routing_peers.label: cloud-superapp

ui._doc_app_mesh: Configs ▸ About ▸ Network ▸ IPC Contract — the inter-app mesh. The apps on this phone talk to each other over Binder, and until now that mesh existed only as constants scattered across the libraries that bind it: nothing anywhere said WHO the peers are. That made a dead peer indistinguishable from a feature that was never wired. This is the roster, one entry per CHANNEL (not per app, because one app can serve several and one channel can have several servers). A $pkg placeholder inside an action or authority means the serving package's own, which is how the two terminal apps each publish the same channel under their own name. Declared here, rendered by DevControlFragment.collectAppMesh with a live verdict per row. What is NOT in here and cannot be: whether the peer is installed, and whether it actually publishes the channel — those are questions for the device, asked at render time, exactly as ui.ai_routing_peers does. Platform bindings (input method, notification listener, call screening, credential provider, accessibility, quick-settings tiles) are deliberately absent: the peer there is Android, not another app of ours.

app_mesh.label: Text Tools
app_mesh.note: Enhance, Translate, Grammar and Resume for every app. Order is PREFERENCE, not a retry chain: the first installed server wins and resolution happens once per bind. Cloud Writer is preferred and deliberately publishes no service yet, so today the keyboard serves.

app_mesh.label: Fleet Token
app_mesh.note: The SuperApp hands its GitHub fleet token to sibling apps so Constellation updates work without every app storing a credential.

app_mesh.label: Autofill SOT
app_mesh.note: The non-secret autofill Source of Truth (a0_docs/eng-specs/autofill-3-tier.md): profiles, per-site form rules and snippets Cloud Account owns. Cloud Browser fills contact/address forms from it and Cloud Keyboard offers its candidates; both hold the signature-level AUTOFILL_PROFILE_READ, and only the browser holds AUTOFILL_PROFILE_WRITE (a user-confirmed new address). Never secrets: those are Cloud Vault's, through the Android Autofill framework.

app_mesh.label: Translate Engine
app_mesh.note: Heavy translation models live in their own APK so the keyboard stays small. Its own permission, not CONSTELLATION_DATA: the engine APK predates that grant.

app_mesh.label: Voice Engine
app_mesh.note: Same APK as the translate engine, same reason.

app_mesh.label: Cloud Exec
app_mesh.note: Lets the SuperApp run a shell command inside the terminal environment. This is how the watchdog and the dev-control surfaces reach the filesystem without shipping their own shell.

app_mesh.label: Terminal Session
app_mesh.note: A login shell in a PTY for Cloud MyTerminal (ICloudSession), the zero-setup replacement for loopback SSH: no sshd, no listening socket, no key to copy. Signature-level, defined by both terminals and MyTerminal so the grant never depends on install order; every call re-checks permission and signature.

app_mesh.label: Run Command
app_mesh.note: The upstream terminal contract, kept because the boot runner uses it. Needs allow-external-apps=true in termux.properties on the serving side (see #198) — a grant this roster cannot see.

app_mesh.label: Terminal Files
app_mesh.note: Document and file access into the terminal home, so other apps can open a file there with the system picker.

app_mesh.label: Shizuku Bridge
app_mesh.note: Shizuku's own discovery provider, published by this app. It is how Shizuku finds us, not how we find Shizuku.

ui._doc_control_panel:
Configs ▸ Launcher ▸ Controls (was Panel ▸ Control, #574) — the switch board, DECLARED here and implemented in configs/DeviceControls.kt. This file owns PRESENTATION ONLY: which controls appear, in which group, in what order, under what wording, and how many tiles fit across. It owns nothing about what a control can do.

THE GROUPS ANSWER 'WHAT AM I LOOKING FOR', NOT 'WHAT WOULD THIS BREAK'. They used to be Phone / Cloud / System, a blast-radius taxonomy: what does flipping this change — the handset, the fleet, or this app. That is a good way to think about consequences and a poor way to FIND something, and finding is the entire errand that brings anybody to a quick-settings grid. Under blast radius the radios were split across two groups (Wi-Fi, mobile data, Bluetooth and airplane mode under Phone; the mesh tunnel and the per-app firewall under Cloud), so 'turn the network off' meant visiting two of the three groups and knowing in advance which half lived where. Device / Network / Tools / UI groups by the thing the owner has in mind when they reach for the page. Every control still lands in exactly one of them; nothing needed an Others.

BATTERY HUNGERS IS A SECOND VIEW, NOT A FIFTH HOME. A group that declares `derive` owns no `controls` array of its own — its rows are every control in the groups above carrying that flag, in declared order. So a battery-hungry control is drawn TWICE, once in its functional group and once here, and both tiles are the same control id, which is the only thing either of them holds. There is no second copy of the state to drift: DeviceControls.byId maps one id to one Control, one read and one write, and ControlFragment repaints EVERY tile bearing an id when that id's reading lands. Adding a control to Battery Hungers is `"battery_hungry": true` on the control and nothing else — no Kotlin, no second list of ids to fall out of step with the first. Removing the whole group is deleting one entry from `groups`. A second derived view (privacy, say) is another entry with another flag and still no Kotlin.

WHAT COUNTS AS BATTERY-HUNGRY is a judgement about mechanism, and it is recorded per control so it can be argued with: a radio that must stay associated (mobile data, Bluetooth), an always-on VpnService (the mesh tunnel, the per-app firewall), a foreground service that polls (the floating menu reads the foreground package once a second), a background sync (fleet auto-update), a continuously animated surface (the shader backdrops behind All animations), the adbd the privileged plane keeps alive (wireless debugging), and the flash unit itself (torch). Auto-brightness is deliberately NOT here — it spends less than a screen pinned bright.

GROUP WORDING IS A STRING RESOURCE, not the text in this file. `label_res` and `subtitle_res` name keys in res/values/strings.xml, resolved at render time, so the group headings reach the owner in Spanish like the rest of the page; `label` and `subtitle` remain as the English fallback and as the documentation of what the key is supposed to say. (The per-CONTROL labels and subtitles below are still raw English text in this file and are NOT translated — a pre-existing gap, 34 strings wide, untouched here.)

NEVER RENDER A SWITCH THAT LIES. Adding an id here does NOT create a control: DeviceControls decides, per control, which of three things it is — (1) really toggleable in-process, so a tile whose state is re-read from the system after every write; (2) toggleable only through a special permission this app holds, so a tile that is DISABLED with the missing permission named on it; (3) not toggleable at all, so a tile that does not switch but opens the exact Settings panel for it and shows the live state read-only. An id declared here with no capability behind it is dropped rather than drawn, because a control that does nothing is the same lie as a switch that does nothing.

control_panel._doc_columns: Tiles across the grid. Data because tile density is the thing the owner re-litigates, and because a column count compiled into Kotlin is a rebuild to argue with. Four is Samsung's own quick-settings width and it is what keeps a tile wide enough to hit: at four columns a 360dp-wide phone gives roughly 80dp of tile, comfortably past the 48dp minimum touch target. Raising this past five starts trading that away.

groups.label: Device
groups.subtitle: The handset's own hardware and attention.

controls.label: Torch
controls.subtitle: The flash unit, straight through CameraManager — no permission needed.

controls.label: Rotation lock
controls.subtitle: Freezes the screen in its current orientation.

groups.label: Network
groups.subtitle: Everything that moves bytes — this handset's radios and the fleet's tunnels, in one place.

controls.label: Wi-Fi
controls.subtitle: Android forbids an app to flip the Wi-Fi radio.

controls.label: Mobile data
controls.subtitle: Carrier data is a system-only switch.

controls.label: Bluetooth
controls.subtitle: The adapter's own enable/disable is a no-op for a normal app.

controls.label: Airplane mode
controls.subtitle: Writable as a setting, but the broadcast that moves the radios is not ours to send — writing it alone changes the icon and nothing else.

controls.label: WireGuard mesh
controls.subtitle: The 10.0.0.x tunnel. Needs the engine APK and VPN consent.

controls.label: Per-app firewall
controls.subtitle: The local no-root VpnService that blocks per-app egress.

groups.label: Tools
groups.subtitle: The machinery this app and the fleet are driven through.

controls.label: Wireless debugging
controls.subtitle: The adbd this app's own privileged plane talks to. Turning it off ends silent installs and self-grants until it is back on.

controls.label: Keep Wireless debugging on
controls.subtitle: Turns Wireless debugging back on whenever Android drops it (Wi-Fi change, reboot) and reconnects the shell channel. Off (the default) leaves it exactly as you set it and the app never connects the channel by itself.

controls.label: App API
controls.subtitle: DevControlServer — the loopback HTTP surface the MCP and every script drive this app through.

controls.label: Fleet auto-update
controls.subtitle: Periodic GHCR check and silent install for every constellation app.

groups.label: UI
groups.subtitle: How this launcher looks and feels under the thumb.

controls.label: Floating menu
controls.subtitle: The draggable overlay button, on top of any app.

controls.label: Admin mode
controls.subtitle: Swaps the Home grid, drawer and bottom-nav to their Admin variants.

controls.label: All animations
controls.subtitle: Master motion gate — off stops every animated surface at once.

groups.label: Battery Hungers
groups.subtitle: The same controls again, gathered so everything draining the battery can be switched off from one row.
groups._doc_details: THE TILES ANSWER 'WHAT IS DRAINING IT THAT I CAN SWITCH OFF'. They do NOT answer 'WHICH APPS ARE EATING MY BATTERY', which is a different question and the one the owner also asked. This group's tiles are a JUDGEMENT recorded per control (see battery_hungry above) — editorial, not measured — and nothing here is a per-app number. The measured answer already exists in this app and was simply unreachable from this page: libs:battery's EnergyUsageDialog, until now openable only from the developer Control page. `details` names the surface a group can hand off to; ControlFragment maps the name to the dialog exactly as Sections.iconResFor maps an icon name to a drawable, and a name it does not know draws no affordance rather than crashing. This is a LINK, not a second copy of the data — a per-app list re-implemented here is the drift that the one-id-one-Control rule above exists to prevent.

ui._doc_notification_center:
Configs ▸ Launcher ▸ Notify ▸ persistent badges (#497; the Push tab until #580 merged it into Notify) — the ONE declaration of every notification-center / badge producer this app ships, and the source the badge panes render verbatim: nothing it lists is invented in Kotlin, and nothing this app draws as a badge or a notification is missing from it. Diego asked for 'the kde badge, the music badge, the quickmarks badge….' and trailed off on purpose — that trailing off is what makes this a declaration instead of his list of three: BadgePanes iterates `producers` and draws whatever is here, so adding or dropping an entry changes the tab with no Kotlin edit, the same contract configs/DeviceControls.kt keeps for Control.

Split exactly like Control/DeviceControls: this file owns PRESENTATION — which producers exist, what each one IS (label/subtitle/icon), which surface it occupies (`surface`: a system notification, an in-app card, or a launcher-icon badge count) and whether it is declared on. The CAPABILITY — the actual channel, the actual notify()/cancel() calls, the actual read of NotificationListenerService — stays owned by that producer's own Kotlin file, named in `owner` below, exactly where DeviceControls keeps a control's read/set next to the declaration that names it.

`enabled` is the declared default of the owner's per-badge switch (BadgeCustomization); since #777 a badge is shown only when its switch AND its group's switch (`groups` below) are on. A producer with no capability behind it — an id with no file in `owner` implementing it — is exactly the DeviceControls failure mode (a row that draws and means nothing), which is why the tester for this page checks `owner` resolves to a real file, not just that the JSON parses.

QUICKMARKS: swept for an actual unread-count badge on Phone ▸ Apps ▸ Quickmarks tiles and found none — AppIconTile draws a 'Not installed' placeholder glyph, not a notification count. What IS real and what an owner would call 'the quickmarks badge' is the system launcher-icon badge every tile can carry, driven by whichever channels below have `shows_badge: true` and cleared when a notification surface calls cancelAll() — declared here as `launcher_icon_badge`, coupled to `phone_notification_listener` rather than invented as a fourth independent mechanism.

notification_center._doc: One entry per PRODUCER. `badge` is what splits a shade badge from the rest of the channel inventory: true means this producer puts a PERSISTENT entry in the notification centre, and Configs > Home > Push renders exactly those — one box in section 1, one customization menu in section 2, derived, never a hand-kept name list. `persistent` means it must survive an app update and a reboot: BadgeRestartReceiver re-ensures every persistent producer's `service` on MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED / BOOT_COMPLETED. Before that existed, only KdeStatusService restarted itself (App.kt) and everything owned by FloatingNavService — Quickmarks, Media, Alerts — stayed dead after an update. `requires` names the grants a badge needs so a dead badge can say WHY instead of reading absent. Adding a badge means adding an entry HERE and nothing else.
notification_center._doc_groups: #777 THE FOUR shade groups of Configs ▸ Launcher ▸ Notify, as data: NotifyGroups gives every member's notification its group's key (setGroup) and posts one summary per group, so the shade shows four bundles instead of seven loose badges. `members` are producer ids below, in the order they sort inside the group; a producer in no group posts ungrouped. Group order and on/off are the owner's (Notify page, stored per group id); the declaration order is the default order. `alerts: true` marks the group whose member is the fleet alerts channel (FleetAlerts → AlertStore → AlertsNotifier); the Notify page draws its filters and Clear all from that flag, never from a name. `max_in_shade` caps how many alert children are posted (the store keeps more; Android drops an app's notifications past ~50). #1113 A GROUP IS ALSO A SECTION OF THE NOTIFY PAGE: the page draws a plain (not collapsible) subtitle with the group label, then the cards of its members in this order, groups in the owner's order, so the shade bundles and the page sections come from this one list (card.rank is no longer read). Section order: Resources (Mesh, Data, Battery), Infos (Weather, Markets, MyHealth), Actions (Quick Actions, KDE Connect), Media (Media Player), Alerts. A future AI badge is a producer id appended to `live` (Infos), with no Kotlin edit.

producers.label: KDE Connect
producers.subtitle: Ongoing 'Cloud SA - KDE' notification plus an in-app card mirroring the paired desktop's connection, battery and plugin state.
producers.shows: Paired desktop name, connection state, battery, plugins.

producers.label: Media Playing
producers.subtitle: The 'Cloud SA - Media' transport badge mirroring the active media session. Pinned even when paused so the transport is always reachable.
producers.shows: Track title, artist, album art, prev/play-pause/next.

customization.label: Keep the badge when nothing is playing

producers.label: Quickmarks
producers.subtitle: The persistent 'Cloud SA - Quick Actions' badge the floating overlay pins while it is running.

producers.label: Alerts
producers.subtitle: #777 The fleet's ONE alerts channel. Every Cloud app raises its user-facing alerts through FleetAlerts (libs:core) and they land here, one child per alert under one 'Cloud SA - Alerts' summary. Only real alerts: an empty store posts nothing. It replaced the 'Grouped alerts' badge, which showed sample data baked from ui.notification_infos.
producers.shows: One row per alert a fleet app raised: app, severity, title, text; tap opens the alert's deep link.

producers.label: Mesh
producers.subtitle: The mesh at a glance (the Mesh badge of the Network group): connected or not, the tunnel, this device's mesh IP, peer count and rx/tx; expanded, the last handshake per peer, the interface and peer addresses, DNS (the mesh DNS, the resolvers Android uses now, the 127.0.0.1 bridge status, Private DNS mode) and uptime. Buttons: Always On (shows the system state, opens the VPN settings where it is switched), Connect/Disconnect, More (the Cloud Mesh page). Read over INetBackend from Cloud-Lib-Net-Wg; refreshed on connect/disconnect and VPN network events, plus every 30s only while connected.
producers.shows: Connected/disconnected, tunnel, mesh IP, peers, rx/tx; expanded: handshakes, addresses, DNS, uptime.

producers.label: Data
producers.subtitle: The Data badge of the Network group: data used today and this month, mobile vs Wi-Fi, and the top apps of the month, all from the Data Manager engine (libs:datamanager, the one behind Configs > About > Data Usage). Buttons: Data Manager (opens it), Refresh; without Usage Access the badge says so and offers Grant access. Read when the screen comes on and on Refresh; nothing polls.
producers.shows: Data today and this month (mobile, Wi-Fi), top apps; Usage Access needed.

producers.label: Battery
producers.subtitle: The battery at a glance, time first: charging shows the time until full, discharging the time until empty from the average drain since the last unplug or full charge (h:mm, labelled as an estimate; 'learning' until 2% is used or 15 min pass). Expanded: level, status and plug, current now and average, voltage, temperature, health, cycles, charge and capacity, time and percent used since the last charge, and the short-term rate. Refreshed on the battery-changed event only; nothing polls.
producers.shows: Time to full or empty (est), level, status, plug, current, voltage, temperature, health, cycles, capacity, time and % since last charge.

producers.label: AI
producers.subtitle: AI usage at a glance (#1151): Claude 5-hour session used % and weekly all-models used % with their reset times, then the OpenRouter balance in dollars and the spend of the last day, 7 days and this month, each in dollars and millions of tokens. Read from c3-infra-api GET /ai/usage (mesh first, then the public address with the fleet bearer): Claude Code pushes its rate limits there from the statusLine poster, OpenRouter is fetched server-side. Read on start, when the screen comes on and every 5 minutes while it is on, and on Refresh. Data older than 15 minutes is marked stale.
producers.shows: Claude session and weekly used % with resets; OpenRouter balance and spend (24h, 7d, month) in $ and M tokens; stale marker.

producers.label: MyHealth
producers.subtitle: Today's steps in km with the step count, resting heart rate and last night's sleep, from the same Health Connect read as Boards > MyHealth. Never estimated; a missing grant shows the reason and a Grant access button. Tap opens Boards > MyHealth.
producers.shows: Steps in km, resting heart rate, last night's sleep.

producers.label: Weather
producers.subtitle: Today where the device is: current temperature, the day's max/min and the hour-by-hour forecast, from Open-Meteo (no key, no account) for the last known position. The place name comes from Android's own geocoder. Location is never actively requested — the badge reads the position someone else already paid for.
producers.shows: Current temp, day max/min and the location name; expands to today's forecast by hour.

producers.label: Markets
producers.subtitle: Live last-traded prices for the declared instruments, from Yahoo Finance. One action button per instrument opens that instrument's Yahoo ticker page in the app's own embedded browser. A quote that could not be fetched reads '—', never the last good number.
producers.shows: Last price per declared instrument, with the age of the quote when it is stale.
producers._doc_instruments: WHAT the badge quotes, as data — symbol is Yahoo's, label is what the owner reads, decimals is how the number is printed, url is the ticker page a tap opens. Changing the four instruments, their order, their captions or their precision is an edit HERE and no Kotlin. `BRL=X` is Yahoo's USD->BRL cross (reais per dollar, ~5.x), so its label says USD/BRL: the number and the caption have to run the same way round or a 5.14 reads as a broken 0.19. Petrol is WTI front-month (CL=F); Brent is BZ=F and is a one-line swap here if the owner wants the global benchmark instead.

producers.label: Phone notification access
producers.subtitle: The NotificationListenerService grant every other phone-notification surface is fed from — Control ▸ Permissions grants it, nothing here can switch it.
producers.not_badge_reason: A listener SOURCE. It posts nothing to the shade.

producers.label: Recovery advisory
producers.subtitle: Install/repair advisories, rate-limited by the updater. #777: raised through FleetAlerts into the Alerts group (STUCK = error, on the HIGH-importance 'fleet_alerts_urgent' channel), no longer a channel of its own.
producers.not_badge_reason: Not a badge of its own: each advisory is one alert inside the Alerts group (fleet_alerts), withdrawn once resolved.

producers.label: Screensaver
producers.subtitle: The silent channel ScreensaverService needs to run as a foreground service while the cover overlay is shown.
producers.not_badge_reason: Foreground-service plumbing that exists only WHILE the screensaver cover is up (started on demand from FloatingNavService.kt:373), then goes away.

producers.label: Launcher icon badge
producers.subtitle: The OS unread-count dot on this app's launcher icon, sourced from whichever channels are shows_badge=true.
producers.not_badge_reason: The home-screen icon dot, not an entry in the notification shade.

ui._doc_floating_nav: Floating Top Nav Bar — a SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW overlay (FloatingNavService) shown whenever the user has left Cloud-SuperApp. Collapsed = a small transparent circle, top-centre; tapped = expands to a top rectangle bar of links. The bar is CONTEXT-AWARE: FloatingNavService polls the foreground package (UsageStatsManager, poll_ms) and picks the first context whose `match_prefixes` matches (prefix = pkg == p || pkg startsWith p + '.'); the `default` context (empty match_prefixes) is the fallback. Each context shows `home_label` (the ✲ primary, brings `home_package` to front — 'self' = Cloud-SuperApp) then its `links` (label → package; tap launches getLaunchIntentForPackage, or installs via `install_app` external_apps id when absent). When the foreground IS Cloud-SuperApp the overlay hides entirely (we're already home). Packages mirror ui.external_apps forks + ui.permissions.roles (Fossy = the comms dialer fork). Add a context / link = edit here; nothing in Kotlin hardcodes a package.

floating_nav._doc_default_on: `enabled` is the BUILD's kill-switch: false removes the feature for everyone, including a user who switched it on. `default_on` is only where the Configs > One-Hand > Floating button switch starts on a device that has never touched it. Off by default: the button is a foreground service drawn over every app, so it is opted into, not opted out of. A user who flipped the switch keeps their choice, because the stored pref is read first and this value is only its fallback.
floating_nav._doc_layout: The expanded menu renders the SAME 3-line box wherever it is triggered (single engine: FloatingNavService.showBar). Line 1 = `root` (the constellation apex, BIGGEST font) = Cloud SuperApp. Line 2 = `parents` (the sibling hubs cloud-myterminal · Cloud Comms · Cloud Nav, medium font), constant everywhere, centred; the hub matching the current foreground app is bold. Line 3 = the `children` of the context matched from the foreground package (cloud-myterminal → Acode·Amaze; Cloud-Comms → Mail·Chat·Messenger·Dialer; Cloud-Nav → none; otherwise the `default` context = Cloud-SuperApp's first-level pages), SMALLEST font. Font size strictly decreases per line (root > parents > children). Layout: `top_offset_dp` = distance from the top edge (renders below the centred island cluster); `width_pct` = box width as % of screen width. Every item has a `target`: `self` brings Cloud-SuperApp home; `app:<pkg>` launches that package (installing the `install_app` companion APK if absent); `section:<id>` / `action:<id>` / `page:<...>` bring Cloud-SuperApp forward and dispatch via its shortcut_action handler (onTileClicked). Bolding of the current hub is data-driven from each context's `match_prefixes` — nothing in Kotlin hardcodes a label or package. Add a hub / child = edit here.

parents.label: Inboxes
parents._doc: The Cloud-Comms hub is decommissioned; its 4 ex-forks are standalone apps. This parent now opens SuperApp's Communications section (Mail/Chat/Messenger/Dialer tiles → extapp:cloud-{mail,chat,matrix,dialer}) instead of launching/installing a dead hub. The `comms` context below still bolds this parent + lists the 4 apps (app:com.diegonmarcos.comms.*) when any is foreground.

floating_nav._doc_actions: Global utility actions, identical in every context. The COMPACT menu shows the first `compact_action_count` (3); the EXPANDED view shows ALL of them (up to 5) plus a now-playing album-art card. Targets: `torch` toggles the flashlight (CameraManager.setTorchMode, no camera perm); `calc` opens Cloud Calc (com.diegonmarcos.cloudcalc), else Cloud Store on its Cloud tab, else the SuperApp Store row (apps/CalcHandoff.kt), never the system calculator; `screensaver` starts ScreensaverService (full-black cover overlay — see ui.screensaver); `lock` locks the screen (ScreenLocker); `action:<id>` routes through Cloud-SuperApp. Add/replace/reorder = edit here.

contexts._doc: Cloud-Nav is a single forkless app, so it has NO child apps — `children` is empty and line 3 is omitted when it is foreground. This context exists only so the Cloud Nav hub on line 2 bolds (match via match_prefixes) when com.diegonmarcos.cloudnav is in the foreground.

ui._doc_kde_connect: KDE Connect config consumed by libs:kde-connect (Configs > KDE page). FULLY SELF-CONTAINED, ORIGINAL (clean-room) implementation of the KDE Connect LAN protocol — NO dependency on org.kde.kdeconnect_tp, NOT its GPL source. Auto-discovery (UDP broadcast / mDNS) does NOT cross WireGuard, so the client connects by explicit wg_ip instead: it dials <wg_ip>:discovery_port (1716) over wg0, writes its identity, runs the KDE Connect mutual-TLS handshake AS THE TLS SERVER (the protocol rule: the side that dials the TCP becomes the TLS server), re-exchanges identity encrypted (protocol v8), then pumps NetworkPackets through the plugin registry (ping/clipboard/findmyphone/notification). Pairing = remembering the peer's certificate; reconnects are cert-pinned. `self_name` is our advertised device name; `package` is retained only for the legacy 'open official app' affordance, never required. `devices[]` = the wg_ip targets we can reach (Surface Pro = mesh node 'laptop' = 10.0.0.5). Add a target = append a device with its wg_ip; nothing in Kotlin hardcodes an IP. The phone running the app advertises itself via self_name (this device = Samsung Galaxy S21 @ wg 10.0.0.9).

kde_connect._doc_plugins: Full KDE Connect plugin catalog, shown on the KDE page. `status`=active means the `packet` IS advertised in our identity capabilities (so the desktop shows the plugin for this device) and the per-plugin toggle controls it. Two flavours of active: (a) HANDLED — a real KdePluginRegistry plugin processes the packet (ping, clipboard, findmyphone, notification, battery, share, mpris, systemvolume, runcommand, contacts, connectivity_report, lockdevice, telephony, + the request-side aliases); (b) ADVERTISED-ONLY STUB — listed + advertised for visibility/testing but with NO Kotlin handler yet, so inbound packets are ignored until a handler lands (sms, mousepad, presenter, sftp, photo, remotekeyboard, bigscreen, virtualmonitor, screenconnector, presenter_remote, sftp_browse, sms_request). The KDE page colours handled (lavender) vs advertised-only (amber). `dir` from the phone's view: in=we receive, out=we send, both. Promote a stub to handled = add a plugin in KdePluginRegistry with its id.
kde_connect._doc_commands: RunCommandPlugin command list — the desktop can trigger these on the phone (kdeconnect.runcommand). `type`: app=launch package `value`; url=open `value` in the browser. Data-driven; add a row, the desktop sees it. No permission needed.

ui._doc_retired_tile_ids: 2026-10-14. A Cloud tile id that was renamed, old -> new, written as <section>/<tile id> exactly as ui.home_apps_tabs / Page.appsExtraTileIds refer to a tile. Sections.appTilesFor follows an old reference to the new tile so a saved or deep-linked reference does not silently drop it. Saved Recently Used entries are keyed by launch TARGET, which did not change, so they need no mapping. Add a row whenever a tile id changes.
ui._doc_tile_columns: SHIPPED DEFAULT icons per row for the Cloud grids (6, unchanged). Overridable per phone by the Configs ▸ Launcher ▸ Controls stepper (`grid_cols_cloud`, 4..8); see GridColumns.
ui._doc_ntfy:
USER vs INFRA channel split for the ntfy registry. The channels are one flat list of snake_case topics upstream, so 'my notifications' and 'the cloud's notifications' arrived indistinguishable in one alphabetical wall. Scope is decided by the topic PREFIX, declared here rather than hardcoded in the fragment (FIRE RULE #6): a new prefix is a build.json edit. Anything unmatched counts as INFRA, so a channel can never silently vanish from the list — it lands in the cloud bucket and is visible enough to classify.

`channels` below IS the ntfy registry's own topics[] list — the source of truth is /home/appuser/git/cloud-u-containers/infra-obs_ntfy/src/build.json::topics (this app's clone lives at cloud-u-android, a SIBLING checkout to cloud-u-containers, not a `a_solutions` submodule of it — a path this comment previously got wrong). Verified 2026-09-06: every one of that registry's 23 topic names is present below; `cloud-sa-notifications` / `fleet_advisory` / `infra_mail-health` are the only extras, and they are legitimately NOT in that registry — they are this app's own advisory-scope channels (see `advisory_topic` below), published by a different mechanism than the fleet's ntfy topic list. There is no automated sync from that JSON into this one yet (the two live in different repos and this task's scope did not include building that pipeline); a topic added to the registry needs a matching manual edit here until one exists.

ntfy._doc_base_url: Origin for PROGRAMMATIC reads (the JSON poll API). This is ntfy itself on the WireGuard mesh. It is NOT rss.diegonmarcos.com: that hostname is the same container behind Caddy, whose only anonymous prefix is /feed* (infra-sec_caddy/src/caddyfile.nix::mkNtfyBlock, feed_auth="none"), and /feed* is served by the rss-gateway sidecar which publishes profiles.json, channels.json and <profile>.atom / c/<topic>.atom — it has no /<topic>/json route at all. Every other path on that host falls through to `handle { forward_auth authelia }` and answers 302 to the SSO portal, which is the 401 the Notify cards rendered. Measured anonymously from a mesh peer on 2026-09-09: /feed/channels.json 200, /feed/<topic>/json 404, /<topic>/json 302 -> auth.diegonmarcos.com, http://10.0.0.6:8090/<topic>/json 200 for all 26 channels below.
ntfy._doc_web_base_url: Origin for HUMAN links — the topic page a card opens in the in-app browser. The public hostname on purpose: a WebView carries the Authelia session cookie and satisfies the gate, which is the tier that exists for people.
ntfy._doc_poll_window: `since` for the channel cards, in a unit ntfy parses — s/m/h, a Unix timestamp, a message id or `all`. NEVER `d`: since=7d answers HTTP 400 {"code":40008}. Kept at a day rather than a week because health_resources alone replays 851 KB / 2101 messages over 24h and 3.6 MB over 168h, and a shade only ever shows the newest handful.

scopes.label: Advisories
scopes.subtitle: Out-of-band install and repair notices — read this first

ntfy._doc_labels: Human titles, loosely mirrored from the fleet's own registry at cloud-u-containers/infra-obs_ntfy/src/build.json::topics[].desc (the source of truth) — reworded for length rather than copied verbatim. A raw snake_case topic is an address, not a name: 'sec_yara' tells you nothing about what arrives there, and a list of twenty-six of them is an inventory nobody reads. A topic with no entry here still renders — under its raw name — because a missing label must degrade to less readable, never to invisible.

labels.fleet_advisory: Fleet advisories · app is stuck, here is the fix

ntfy._doc_taxon: Section PREFIX per cloud publisher, in the same one-character vocabulary ui.phone_sections declares ("_" Sys, "@" Inboxes & AI, "." Data Apps, "=" Primary, ">" Media, "*" Health, "-"/"+" Services). The Notify tabs narrow phone groups by running PhoneAppClassifier over each package, but a cloud message carries no package — only an ntfy topic or an in-app producer name — so there is nothing to classify and this map is the classification. Without it every cloud publisher passed the taxonomy filter untouched and the SuperApp updater appeared on all six tabs, listed under Inboxes and under Data Apps as readily as under Sys. A key that is NOT declared here shows on the All tab only: a publisher nobody has categorised must not silently claim a category. Keys are matched against the group key, which is the topic for a channel and NotificationStore.source for the in-app feed.

ui._doc_c3_ops: Where the C3 container sheet's Actions tab POSTs. c3-infra-api's operations routes, reached through the same public base the front portal uses. The API distinguishes a CONTAINER from its SERVICE — /vms/{vm}/containers/{name}/{start,stop,restart,update} against /vms/{vm}/services/{service}/{start,stop} — which is why the sheet shows Container Actions and App Actions as two lists rather than one: they are two different operations with different blast radius, and the infrastructure already says so. AUTHENTICATED: this path is behind Caddy forward_auth, so every call carries the Authelia bearer libs:ops already stores for Dagu. Empty base_url disables the Actions tab's network buttons and says so; Infos needs no network at all.

deploy.note: APK produced in dist/. Side-loadable via adb or shared via Filebrowser.

release._doc: Data-driven publish targets for the APK. build.sh oras-push + build.sh gh-release read this block; the GHA workflow (1_cicd/src/cicd/ship-cloud-superapp.yml) invokes those engine commands — no hardcoded registry/tag strings in the workflow.

artifact._doc: Path under dist/ to publish. The `debug` key is the daily-driver build (R8 shrink-only since 2026-08-21 - minifyEnabled true with -dontobfuscate, so names/line numbers and therefore real stacktraces survive while unreachable library code is dropped; debug keystore) — it is THE app for this stack, not a side-by-side dev variant. The `release` key exists for when a true Play-Store-style release lifecycle lands; the GHA workflow picks debug for main pushes.

release._doc_variants: Per-ABI build variants. The CI workflow runs one job per variant (matrix); the engine reads SUPERAPP_VARIANT to override the ABI filter (→ gradle env SUPERAPP_ABIS), the dist artifact name, the GHCR tag suffix, and the GitHub-release asset name. `arm64` is the DEFAULT — when SUPERAPP_VARIANT is unset the engine behaves exactly as before (arm64-v8a, Cloud-SuperApp.apk, ghcr :latest). `x86_64` adds a parallel artifact for Waydroid / desktop emulators, published to the SAME rolling `latest` GitHub release under a distinct filename, and to GHCR under tag suffix `-x86_64`. `supported_abis` drives the updater's ABI→tag map (AUTO_UPDATE_TAG_MAP, baked in libs/updater): a device resolves its update tag by the first Build.SUPPORTED_ABIS entry that matches — native ABIs precede libhoudini-translated ones, so an x86_64 Waydroid correctly pulls `latest-x86_64`. `update_tag` MUST equal `latest` + `ghcr_tag_suffix` so the updater and the publisher agree. Add an ABI = append a variant here; no Kotlin/gradle/workflow edits beyond the matrix list.

ghcr._doc: ORAS push as an OCI artifact (not a container — APK is a blob). One :latest tag plus per-commit sha + per-version tags. Image renamed from `superapp` to `cloud-superapp` — old package becomes orphan.

gh_release._doc: GitHub Release attachment. rolling_tag is the canonical mode now: one release named (default `latest`) the ship workflow overwrites on every main push, so the linktree Android download link stays stable. tag_pattern stays as legacy for immutable per-tag releases when invoked under a tag push context (rolling release still publishes alongside).

phone_install._doc: Targets for build.sh phone-install. Pulls APK from GHCR via curl+OCI HTTP API (no oras dep — works on aarch64 Termux without a Nix shell) and copies to a target dir an Android file manager can see. Override target_dir per environment via PHONE_TARGET env var; default suits Termux/nix-on-droid where ~/storage symlinks to /storage/emulated/0/.

auto_update._doc: In-app updater config — read at gradle eval time into BuildConfig, then used by libs:updater at runtime. Same registry/namespace/image as release.ghcr (the engine asserts consistency at build time).
auto_update._doc_interval: WorkManager periodic minimum is 15 min. 6h matches typical update cadence + spares battery / data.
auto_update._doc_unmetered: true → automatic auto-download+install only on unmetered (Wi-Fi). On a metered network (mobile data) an automatic run does NOT download; it shows the 'Update available — Update now / Later' prompt so the user consents before spending data. Manual 'Check for updates' and the prompt's 'Update now' force a download on any network.
auto_update._doc_install: Declared default for the runtime Auto-update toggle (Configs/About → Permissions, user-overridable via AutoUpdatePrefs). 'silent' → installer commits with USER_ACTION_NOT_REQUIRED (no install prompt) once the one-time 'Install unknown apps' grant is given; without the grant Android transparently falls back to a prompt. 'prompt' → always USER_ACTION_REQUIRED.
auto_update._doc_max_installs_per_pass: Most install sessions ONE unattended background pass may open. A background pass cannot show the system install dialog (Android 10+ blocks background activity starts), so each install it starts leaves a tap-to-install notification holding a PackageInstaller session until the user answers it. Unbounded, one pass over the 40-entry fleet opens 40 and the installer hits Android's 50-session cap - 'Too many active sessions for UID'. The remainder is picked up by the next pass. User-initiated 'Update all' is NOT capped: it runs in the foreground where the dialog appears and sessions resolve at once.

apk_cache._doc: #625 WHERE A DOWNLOADED APK LIVES BETWEEN FETCH AND INSTALL, and when it may be deleted. Read at gradle eval time into libs:updater's BuildConfig (APK_CACHE_DIR / APK_CACHE_MAX_BYTES / APK_CACHE_EVICT) and used by ApkCache at runtime, so the policy exists once, here, and never as a constant in Kotlin. FLEET-WIDE: libs:updater resolves this block from the CONSUMING app's build.json and falls back to THIS file, the same way it resolves constellation-fleet.json — an app may narrow the policy, none has to restate it.
apk_cache._doc_dir: Subdirectory under the app's no_backup files dir (NOT cacheDir). cacheDir is reclaimable: Android purges it under storage pressure without asking and Settings ▸ Clear cache wipes it, so a 267 MB download really did vanish between fetch and install — which is exactly the 'the store deleted my download' the owner reported. no_backup is app-private, persistent, and excluded from cloud backup, so nothing but this app's own retention rule removes an APK.
apk_cache._doc_max_bytes: #812 The cache bound is DERIVED, not fixed: (real free storage on the cache volume + what the cache holds - reserve_bytes), clamped to [min_bytes, max_bytes]. The fixed 1 GiB bound said 'no room' on a phone with ~40 GB free and evicted downloaded-but-not-installed APKs (the two rootfs libs alone are ~1 GB), so Download all re-fetched in a loop. Eviction takes only superseded or already-installed entries, never one pending install. reserve_bytes is what a download may never eat into.
apk_cache._doc_evict: superseded-then-oldest: an entry for a package that also has a NEWER cached build goes first (it can never be installed again), then the oldest by mtime. An entry with no download record — a .part, or a file whose sidecar is gone — is UNVERIFIED and is only ever taken as a last resort, and when it is, it is named in the log and in the eviction report. Silently deleting a file nobody can vouch for is the bug this whole block exists to end.

analytics._doc: Consumed by :libs:analytics, which reads THIS file (rootDir) at build time and bakes the values into BuildConfig. Both backends are single-site today, so every app reports into the same site and is told apart by .app — give each app its own site_id once per-app sites exist in Umami/Matomo.

perms._doc: #1360 every grant this app needs, by libs:perms catalogue id (needs), and the fleet apps that do work for it with the grants THEY must hold (helpers). The ONE declaration: generated into assets/app-perms.json (cloud-android-perms-guard.py --write), drawn by Configs > General > Perms (libs:perms AppPermsSection) with live state, Grant / Open and Grant all, asked at first run (first_run), and reported as 'Missing permission X - Grant' when an operation fails (PermsGate). perms-guard fails when code uses a gated API or another app's engine that is not declared here, or when the manifest and this list disagree.
